text:
Andy Burnham has criticised former prime ministers for being “stuck in the past” amid warnings over re-opening the Brexit debate, with informal talks now set to take place with Brussels about how the UK could forge even closer ties with the EU.
After a major summit between UK and EU leaders on Friday when trade and youth mobility deals were struck, Brussels signalled a willingness to begin “brainstorming” sessions with UK officials and ministers about the shape of the future relationship, including options of a Swiss-style deal with close sectoral alignment, a single market and customs union deal or a path for Britain to rejoin the EU as a full member.
Burnham said there would now be discussions in the run-up to the next summit, which is expected to result in a deal brokered on UK participation in the EU’s internal electricity market, and political dialogue on a longer-term, deeper relationship.
Officials in both the EU and UK have signalled they would like to see those discussions with Brussels run in parallel to the “national debate” that Burnham has said he wishes to have with the UK public about what the closer future relationship might look like.
Burnham said the food and drink deal signed with the EU on Friday would directly cut costs for shoppers and dismissed the advice of former prime ministers, including Rishi Sunak, David Cameron and Theresa May who have said he should not reignite the Brexit debate.
“I’m not sure they’re the people I’ll be listening to here because they left Britain with a bad Brexit deal,” he said. “They’re stuck in the past because they can’t face up to the bad deal that they did.
“I’m not a prime minister that’s going to be stuck in the past. I want to lead Britain forward to a more hopeful future, get the economy growing again, get cost of living down for people, lower energy bills.
“All of these things can be achieved by a more positive, constructive relationship with the European Union. I believe it will be better for Britain to take this path, and I won’t be listening to those voices who put us here in the first place.”
The legal text of the deal, expected in the coming days, is also likely to contain a clause which would penalise the UK if it reneged on the deal in order to pay the costs of reinstating customs infrastructure – which opposition parties have dubbed a “Farage clause” should the Reform UK leader win the next election and reverse the deal.
Burnham, who will lay legislation next week to implement the food and drink deal, said that major supermarkets had confirmed it would “lift the pressure off the weekly shop”.
Speaking at a Morrison’s distribution centre, he said: “They’ve just shown me a stack of paperwork which they have to fill in when they export from here to their store in Gibraltar.
“If you remove that paperwork, that red tape, you can lower the cost, and they say it will lower the pressure on the weekly shop.”
Jukka Salovaara, the EU ambassador to the UK, told reporters on Monday that the agreements would have a direct impact on ordinary people. “The big beneficiaries are young people, businesses and farmers. Removing these barriers should lead to more trade on both sides and increased UK exports.
“What is made in Great Britain will be good to go for the EU market. UK companies exporting to the EU will no longer have to pay the associated carbon charge. This is a major benefit for UK businesses.”
